name: Trader test battery, version 3
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries. Number sequences, probability at speed, and likelihood ranking with intervals.
description: These are reported formats from the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries, as described by Nov 2026. There are three papers, each on its own clock. Sequences is 15 questions in 25 minutes, one at a time, with no skipping. Probability at speed is 15 questions in 30 minutes; you may move between them. Likelihood ranking and intervals is 10 questions in 10 minutes. Wrong answers score 0, and no calculator is allowed. Firms mix and rename these papers, so expect a different order on the day. This is version 3 of 3.

items.title: Equal gaps
items.question: What comes next? 52, 45, 38, 31, 24, ?

options.why: You took the gap of 7 away twice.
You were one out. Check the last step again.
You added 7 instead of taking it away.

feedback.correct: The gap is −7 each time.
feedback.generic: Find the gap between neighbours, with its sign.

explain.text: Each term is 7 less than the one before. So the next is $24 - 7 = 17$.

items.title: A constant ratio
items.question: What comes next? 4, 12, 36, 108, 324, ?

options.why: You were one out. Multiply the last term again.
You multiplied by 2. Each term is 3 times the one before.
You added the last gap of 216 again. The gaps grow too.

feedback.correct: Each term is 3 times the one before.
feedback.generic: Divide each term by the one before it.

explain.text: The ratio is 3 throughout. So the next is $3 \times 324 = 972$.

items.title: Squares shifted
items.question: What comes next? 19, 28, 39, 52, 67, ?

options.why: You added the last gap of 15 again. The gaps grow by 2.
You gave $9^2$ and dropped the +3.
You doubled the last term. The gaps grow by 2, so look for squares.

feedback.correct: Each term is a square plus 3: $9^2 + 3 = 84$.
feedback.generic: Compare each term with the nearest square.

explain.text: The terms are $n^2 + 3$ for $n = 4$ to $8$. The next is $9^2 + 3 = 84$. Check: the gaps rise by 2, so the next gap is 17.

items.title: Double and adjust
items.question: What comes next? 5, 7, 11, 19, 35, ?

options.why: You doubled 35 and left out the −3.
You repeated the last gap of 16. The gaps double.
You doubled and then added 3: the sign is wrong.

feedback.correct: Double, then take away 3.
feedback.generic: Try doubling each term and see what is left over.

explain.text: Each term is double the one before, minus 3. So the next is $2 \times 35 - 3 = 67$. Check: the gaps double, so the next gap is 32.

items.title: Growing gaps
items.question: What comes next? 3, 8, 17, 30, 47, ?

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 17. The gaps grow by 4.
You doubled the last term. Look at the gaps instead.
You were one out. Each gap is 4 more than the last.

feedback.correct: The gaps grow by 4: the next gap is 21.
feedback.generic: Write down the gaps, then the gaps between the gaps.

explain.text: The gaps are 5, 9, 13, 17, rising by 4 each time. So the next gap is 21 and the next term is $47 + 21 = 68$.

options.why: You took away 5 again. The steps take turns: $\times 2$, then $-5$.
You were one out: $2 \times 13 = 26$.
You added the last two terms. The steps take turns.

feedback.correct: The steps take turns, $\times 2$ then $-5$. Next is $\times 2$.
feedback.generic: Look at the steps one at a time: they are not all the same kind.

explain.text: The steps go $\times 2$, $-5$, $\times 2$, $-5$ in turn. The next step is $\times 2$, so $13 \times 2 = 26$.

items.title: Sum of the two before
items.question: What comes next? 2, 7, 9, 16, 25, 41, ?

options.why: You doubled the last term. Add the two before instead.
You repeated the last gap of 16.
You were one out. Add the last two terms again.

feedback.correct: Each term is the sum of the two before: $25 + 41 = 66$.
feedback.generic: Add two neighbours and compare with the term after them.

explain.text: Each term is the sum of the two before it. So the next is $25 + 41 = 66$. Check: the gaps are the earlier terms, so the next gap is 25.

options.why: You doubled the last term. The two lists take turns.
You added 4 to 9, not 3.
You applied the odd-place rule, −4. The eighth term is an even place.

feedback.correct: Two lists take turns. The even places go +3, so $9 + 3 = 12$.
feedback.generic: Read every other term on its own.

explain.text: The odd places go 40, 36, 32, 28, and the even places go 3, 6, 9. The eighth term is an even place, so it is $9 + 3 = 12$.

options.why: You added only the units digit, 7.
You doubled the last term.
You repeated the last gap of 11.

feedback.correct: Add the digit sum: $67 + 13 = 80$.
feedback.generic: Compare each gap with the digits of the term before it.

explain.text: Each gap is the digit sum of the term before: $26 + 8 = 34$, and so on. The last term 67 has digit sum 13, so the next is 80.

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 2, but 75 is not prime.
You doubled the last term. These are the primes in order.
You added 4, but $77 = 7 \times 11$.

feedback.correct: These are the primes in order. The next prime after 73 is 79.
feedback.generic: Each term is a number with a special property. Which numbers are missing?

explain.text: Every term is prime and none is skipped. After 73, the numbers 74, 75, 76, 77, 78 are not prime, so the next is 79.

options.why: You gave $8^3$ and dropped the +2.
You doubled the last term. Compare the terms with the cubes.
You repeated the last gap of 127. The gaps grow faster each time.

feedback.correct: Each term is a cube plus 2: $8^3 + 2 = 514$.
feedback.generic: Compare each term with 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, ...

explain.text: The terms are $n^3 + 2$ for $n = 3$ to $7$. So the next is $8^3 + 2 = 512 + 2 = 514$.

items.title: Two ratios in turn
items.question: What comes next? 3, 1, 6, 4, 12, 16, 24, ?

options.why: You added the last two terms.
You applied the odd-place rule, $\times 2$. The eighth term is an even place.
You doubled 16. The even places go $\times 4$.

feedback.correct: The even places go $\times 4$, so $16 \times 4 = 64$.
feedback.generic: Read the odd places and the even places as two lists.

explain.text: The odd places go 3, 6, 12, 24 ($\times 2$). The even places go 1, 4, 16 ($\times 4$). The eighth term is an even place: $16 \times 4 = 64$.

options.why: You squared 21. Each term is two neighbours multiplied.
You doubled the last term.
You repeated the last gap of 38. The gaps grow by 2.

feedback.correct: Each term is $n(n + 1)$: $20 \times 21 = 420$.
feedback.generic: Write each term as a product of two whole numbers close together.

explain.text: The terms are $15 \times 16$, $16 \times 17$, and so on. So the next is $20 \times 21 = 420$. Check: the gaps rise by 2, so the next gap is 40.

items.title: A rising multiplier
items.question: What comes next? 1, 3, 10, 41, 206, ?

options.why: You multiplied by 6 and left out the + 1.
You kept the multiplier at 5. It rises by 1 each step.
You repeated the last gap of 165.

feedback.correct: Multiply by a number that rises by 1 each step, then add 1: $6 \times 206 + 1 = 1{,}237$.
feedback.generic: Divide each term by the one before. What do the ratios do?

explain.text: The chain is $2 \times 1 + 1 = 3$, $3 \times 3 + 1 = 10$, $4 \times 10 + 1 = 41$, $5 \times 41 + 1 = 206$. The multiplier rises by 1 each step, so the next is $6 \times 206 + 1 = 1{,}237$.

items.title: Sum of the three before
items.question: What comes next? 3, 1, 5, 9, 15, 29, 53, ?

options.why: You added only the last two terms. Each term is the sum of three.
You repeated the last gap of 24.
You doubled the last term.

feedback.correct: Each term is the sum of the three before: $15 + 29 + 53 = 97$.
feedback.generic: Try adding two terms, then three, and compare with the next.

explain.text: From the fourth term on, each is the sum of the three before it. So the next is $15 + 29 + 53 = 97$. Check: $53 \times 2 - 9 = 97$ gives the same.

items.title: A total of 6
items.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the chance that the total is 6?

options.why: You counted each pair twice. There are 5 ordered pairs, not 10.
You found the chance that the total is not 6.
You treated the 11 totals as equally likely. A middle total has more ways.

feedback.correct: 5 of the 36 ordered pairs make 6.
feedback.generic: List the ordered pairs that make the total, out of 36.

items.title: Exactly 4 heads in 5
items.question: A fair coin is tossed 5 times. What is the chance of exactly 4 heads?

options.why: You took 4 heads out of 5 tosses as the chance.
You counted one order only. There are $\binom{5}{4} = 5$ orders.
You found the chance of anything but exactly 4 heads.

feedback.correct: $\binom{5}{4} = 5$ orders, each $\tfrac{1}{32}$.
feedback.generic: Count the orders, then multiply by the chance of one order.

explain.text: There are $\binom{5}{4} = 5$ orders, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{32}$. So the chance is $\tfrac{5}{32} = \tfrac{5}{32}$. Listing all 32 sequences finds the same 5.

items.title: At least one heart in three
items.question: A card is drawn from a full deck and put back, three times. What is the chance of at least one heart?

options.why: You added $\tfrac14$ three times. That counts two hearts twice.
You found the chance that every card is a heart.
You found the chance of no heart at all.

feedback.correct: One minus the chance of no heart: $1 - \tfrac{27}{64}$.
feedback.generic: Find the chance of no heart first.

explain.text: No heart has chance $(\tfrac34)^3 = \tfrac{27}{64}$. So at least one heart is $\tfrac{37}{64}$. Counting all $52^3$ draws gives the same share.

items.title: A heart after a spade
items.question: Two cards are dealt from a full deck. The first is a spade. What is the chance that the second is a heart?

options.why: You put the first card back. With a spade gone, 13 of 51 are hearts.
You took a heart out, but the card gone was a spade.
You found the chance of a spade then a heart, not the second given the first.

feedback.correct: All 13 hearts are left among 51 cards.
feedback.generic: Take the first card out, then count the hearts left.

explain.text: A spade has gone, so all 13 hearts remain among 51 cards: $\tfrac{13}{51}$. Check: spade then heart is $\tfrac{13}{52} \cdot \tfrac{13}{51} = \tfrac{13}{204}$, and dividing by $\tfrac14$ gives $\tfrac{13}{51}$.

items.title: One suit, no hearts
items.question: The hearts are taken out of a deck, leaving 39 cards. Two cards are dealt. What is the chance they share a suit?

options.why: You dealt with replacement. With one card gone, 12 of 38 match.
You found the chance of two of one named suit.
You named one suit and dealt with replacement.

feedback.correct: The first card sets the suit; 12 of the 38 left match it.
feedback.generic: Let the first card choose the suit, then count the matches left.

explain.text: The first card sets the suit, and 12 of the 38 cards left match it: $\tfrac{12}{38} = \tfrac{6}{19}$. Counting pairs: $3\binom{13}{2} = 234$ of $\binom{39}{2} = 741$ agree.

items.title: A paid reroll
items.question: You roll a fair die and win its face in pounds. You may pay £1 to reroll once, then keep the new face. Playing well, what is your expected profit in pounds?

options.why: You averaged only the faces you keep, 3 to 6.
You never rerolled. A 1 or a 2 is worth rerolling, even for £1.
You forgot the £1 fee. It makes a 3 worth keeping.

feedback.correct: A reroll is worth £3.50 less £1. Keep 3 or more.
feedback.generic: A reroll is worth its average less the fee. Keep anything above that.

explain.text: A reroll is worth $3.5 - 1 = 2.5$, so keep 3 to 6. Then $\tfrac{3 + 4 + 5 + 6}{6} + \tfrac26 \cdot \tfrac52 = \tfrac{23}{6}$. Trying every keep rule gives the same best.

items.title: Four birth months
items.question: Four people each have a birth month, all 12 equally likely. What is the chance that all four months differ?

options.why: You multiplied in a fourth factor, $\tfrac{8}{12}$. The first person is free.
You found the chance that two or more share a month.
You took off $\tfrac{1}{12}$ for each of six pairs. The pairs overlap, so that is not exact.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{11}{12} \cdot \tfrac{10}{12} \cdot \tfrac{9}{12} = \tfrac{55}{96}$.
feedback.generic: Add the people one at a time. Each must avoid the months already used.

explain.text: The others avoid 1, 2 and 3 months in turn: $\tfrac{11}{12} \cdot \tfrac{10}{12} \cdot \tfrac{9}{12} = \tfrac{55}{96}$. Counting: $12 \cdot 11 \cdot 10 \cdot 9 = 11880$ of $12^4 = 20736$.

items.title: First ace on the second
items.question: Cards are drawn with replacement until the first ace. What is the chance that the first ace is the second card?

options.why: You used only the second card. The first must miss as well.
You made both cards aces.
You found at least one ace in two cards.

feedback.correct: A miss then an ace: $\tfrac{12}{13} \cdot \tfrac{1}{13}$.
feedback.generic: Write the draws in order: what must the first one do?

explain.text: The first card misses and the second is an ace: $\tfrac{12}{13} \cdot \tfrac{1}{13} = \tfrac{12}{169}$. Listing the 169 rank pairs gives 12 of that shape.

items.title: One bank of two
items.question: A fund picks 2 of 8 stocks at random: 5 tech and 3 banks. What is the chance of exactly 1 bank?

options.why: You counted one order only, bank then tech. There are 2 orders.
You picked with replacement, as if one stock could be chosen twice.
You found the chance of two of a kind.

feedback.correct: $3 \cdot 5 = 15$ pairs of $\binom82 = 28$.
feedback.generic: Count the pairs that fit, then divide by all pairs.

explain.text: Choose 1 of 3 banks and 1 of 5 tech stocks: 15 of $\binom82 = 28$ pairs, so $\tfrac{15}{28}$. Listing all 28 pairs finds the same 15.

items.title: Three red
items.question: An urn holds 4 red and 4 blue balls. You draw 3 without replacement. What is the chance all three are red?

options.why: You found the chance that at least one is blue.
You drew with replacement. Each red drawn leaves fewer reds.
You found three of one colour, either colour.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac48 \cdot \tfrac37 \cdot \tfrac26 = \tfrac{1}{14}$.
feedback.generic: Multiply the chances, removing each red as it is drawn.

explain.text: The chances are $\tfrac48$, then $\tfrac37$, then $\tfrac26$, which multiply to $\tfrac{1}{14}$. Counting: $\binom43 = 4$ of $\binom83 = 56$ sets.

items.title: Flagged orders
items.question: 2% of orders are spoofs. A filter flags 90% of spoofs, and 4% of other orders. An order is flagged. What is the chance it is a spoof?

options.why: You gave the base rate and ignored the flag.
You gave the hit rate: the chance of a flag given a spoof.
You divided the true flags by every order, not by every flag.

feedback.correct: Of 10,000 orders, 180 true flags and 392 false: $\tfrac{180}{572}$.
feedback.generic: Picture 10,000 orders. How many are flagged, and how many of those are spoofs?

explain.text: In 10,000 orders, 200 are spoofs and 180 are flagged; 9,800 are not and 392 are flagged. So $\tfrac{180}{572} = \tfrac{45}{143}$. Bayes' rule gives $\tfrac{0.018}{0.018 + 0.0392}$, the same.

items.title: The larger face is 5
items.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the chance that the larger face is 5? (A double 5 counts.)

options.why: You counted unordered pairs, so (1, 5) and (5, 1) became one.
You found the chance that both are at most 5. Take away both at most 4.
You treated the six values of the larger face as equally likely.

feedback.correct: Both at most 5, less both at most 4: $\tfrac{25 - 16}{36}$.
feedback.generic: Find the chance that both are at most 5, then take away both at most 4.

explain.text: Both at most 5 has 25 pairs; both at most 4 has 16. So the larger is exactly 5 in 9 pairs: $\tfrac{9}{36} = \tfrac14$. Listing the 36 pairs finds the same 9.

items.title: A 5, given 10
items.question: Two fair dice are rolled and the total is 10. What is the chance that at least one die shows 5?

options.why: You listed unordered pairs as equally likely. Ordered pairs are.
You ignored the total. That is the chance of a 5 on any roll.
You did not condition. That is the chance of the total and a 5 together.

feedback.correct: 1 of the 3 ordered pairs that make 10 show a 5.
feedback.generic: List the ordered pairs that make 10. Count those with a 5.

explain.text: The total 10 comes from (4, 6), (5, 5), (6, 4). One of those 3 shows a 5, so $\tfrac{1}{3}$.

items.title: Three players, first six
items.question: Three players take turns to roll a die, you first. The first to roll a six wins. What is your chance of winning?

options.why: You counted only your first roll.
You found the second player's chance.
You ignored going first. The first roller has the edge.

feedback.generic: Win now, or all three miss and the game starts again.

explain.text: Let $p$ be your chance: $p = \tfrac16 + \tfrac{125}{216}p$, so $p = \tfrac{36}{91}$. The series $\tfrac16 \sum (\tfrac{125}{216})^k$ gives the same.

items.title: HHH or THH
items.question: A fair coin is tossed until HHH or THH appears. What is the chance that HHH comes first?

options.why: You treated the two patterns as equal. A T before the first HH sets up THH.
You needed only HH at the start. The third toss must be H as well.
You found the chance that THH comes first.

feedback.correct: HHH wins only if the first three tosses are HHH.
feedback.generic: What happens if a T comes before the first HHH?

explain.text: If any T comes first, the next HH after it completes THH before HHH. So HHH wins only on HHH at the start, with chance $\tfrac18$. An exact solve over the coin's states gives $\tfrac18$ too.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in 5 rolls of a die
A total of 8 or more on two dice

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.667, 0.598, 0.417.
feedback.generic: Work out each chance roughly; a complement is often quickest.

explain.text: A die shows 3 or more: 0.667. At least one six in 5 rolls of a die: 0.598. A total of 8 or more on two dice: 0.417.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: One card from a deck is an ace or a picture card
At least one heart in 2 cards drawn with replacement

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.438, 0.308, 0.250.
feedback.generic: Turn each event into a fraction, then compare.

explain.text: At least one heart in 2 cards drawn with replacement: 0.438. One card from a deck is an ace or a picture card: 0.308. Exactly 3 heads in 4 tosses: 0.250.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one ace in 4 cards dealt from a deck
Three tosses all land the same way
A total of 5 or 10 on two dice

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.281, 0.250, 0.194.
feedback.generic: Use complements for the at-least-one events, and do not add chances.

explain.text: At least one ace in 4 cards dealt from a deck: 0.281. Three tosses all land the same way: 0.250. A total of 5 or 10 on two dice: 0.194.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.402, 0.347, 0.296.
feedback.generic: Count the ways for each, then divide by the outcomes.

explain.text: Exactly one six in 6 rolls: 0.402. Exactly one six in 3 rolls: 0.347. Exactly two sixes in 12 rolls: 0.296.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Two of 25 people share a birthday
At least one double six in 36 rolls of two dice
At least one ace in 8 cards dealt from a deck

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.637, 0.569, 0.499.
feedback.generic: Estimate each with a complement: one minus the chance of none.

explain.text: At least one double six in 36 rolls of two dice: 0.637. Two of 25 people share a birthday: 0.569. At least one ace in 8 cards dealt from a deck: 0.499.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one 5 or 6 in 3 rolls of a die
At least two 5s or 6s in 6 rolls
At least three 5s or 6s in 9 rolls

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.704, 0.649, 0.623.
feedback.generic: Do not assume the events tie because the expected counts match.

explain.text: At least one 5 or 6 in 3 rolls of a die: 0.704. At least two 5s or 6s in 6 rolls: 0.649. At least three 5s or 6s in 9 rolls: 0.623.

items.title: A square root
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $\sqrt{700}$.

options.why: This sits wholly below the value, 26.46.
This holds the value, but 26 to 27 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly above the value, 26.46.

feedback.correct: 26 to 27 holds the value, 26.46, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $26^2 = 676$ and $27^2 = 729$, so $\sqrt{700}$ lies between 26 and 27. In fact $\sqrt{700} = 10\sqrt7 \approx 26.46$. The interval 25 to 30 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Compound growth
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $1.05^{20}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 2.6 to 2.7 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 2.653.
This sits wholly above the value, 2.653.

feedback.correct: 2.6 to 2.7 holds the value, 2.653, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $1.05^{14} \approx 1.98$ by the rule of 72, and $1.05^6 \approx 1.34$. Their product is about 2.65; the exact value is 2.653. The interval 2 to 3 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: Ten losses in a row
items.question: A trade wins a quarter of the time. Choose the tightest interval that holds the chance of 10 losses in a row, $0.75^{10}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 0.05 to 0.06 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 0.05631.
This sits wholly above the value, 0.05631.

feedback.correct: 0.05 to 0.06 holds the value, 0.05631, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $0.75^5 \approx 0.237$, and squaring gives about 0.056. The exact value is 0.0563. The interval 0.02 to 0.10 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: Exactly half heads
items.question: A coin is tossed 30 times. Choose the tightest interval that holds the chance of exactly 15 heads, $\binom{30}{15} / 2^{30}$.

options.why: This sits wholly below the value, 0.1445.
This holds the value, but 0.13 to 0.16 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly above the value, 0.1445.

feedback.correct: 0.13 to 0.16 holds the value, 0.1445, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: For $n$ tosses, exactly half heads is about $\sqrt{2 / (\pi n)}$, which is 0.146 for 30. The exact value is 0.144. The interval 0.1 to 0.3 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

parts.detail: Tick this only if you sat all three papers without one.
